text.p: Italians, long used to skulduggery and political intrigue, on Sunday speculated on who might have bugged the office of former centre-right prime minister Silvio Berlusconi.

The media billionaire, prime minister for seven stormy months in 1994, told a news conference on Friday that a matchbox-sized radio microphone had been found two days earlier taped behind a radiator in his Rome office.
Berlusconi held up the device for photographers, saying it was in perfect working order and capable of transmitting conversations across a range of 300 metres.
He did not blame anyone directly and security experts rejected any involvement of the secret services.
The left-wing daily L'Unita quoted the technician who found the device as saying that it was attached loosely to the radiator with adhesive and was clearly a hasty job.

Another eavesdropping expert named as "Filippo" told the newspaper that the bug looked like something from the 1970s and he doubted whether such primitive items had been used by security services in the last 10 years.
Berlusconi said his lawyer Giuseppe De Luca had been instructed to make an offical complaint to police on Monday, opening the way for a formal criminal inquiry.
President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro asked Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano for a report while centre-left Prime Minister Romano Prodi promised "an exhaustive investigation."

Berlusconi's disclosure sparked a chorus of cross-party outrage, with some centre-right politicians openly comparing the affair to the Watergate political bugging scandal of 1974 that led to the resignation of U.S. president Richard Nixon.
However the initial outcry calmed somewhat on Sunday, with some commentators questioning why Berlusconi had waited two days to announce the discovery of the device.

"More than a re-edition of the Watergate scandal this seems like a complete cock-up,' commented L'Unita, adding that Berlusconi had probably also destroyed any fingerprint evidence by handling the device in front of the media.
Conspiracy theorists, never hard to find in Italy, meanwhile enjoyed a field day -- aided by the fact that Berlusconi's interests span politics and global big business.
Berlusconi is also on trial in Milan for alleged bribes paid by his Fininvest business empire in return for lenient audits and has been mentioned in anti-Mafia investigations.

Some politicians pointed the finger at anti-corruption magistrates, while others suggested politically-motivated rogue elements might be at work in the secret services. Still others detected signs of a foreign hand.

The elite Milan "Clean Hands" pool of anti-corruption magistrates added to the climate of unease by publicly accusing the finance police of "serious irregularities" in relation to a corruption case involving La Spezia magistrates.
Former Justice Minister Filippo Mancuso said he had no doubt that the bug was a case of political espionage.

Mancuso, who said he believed his telephone was also monitored, was quoted in the right-wing daily Il Giornale as saying the country needed shock treatment and suggested Scalfaro should ultimately resign over the affair.
Roberto Maroni of the separatist Northern League, an interior minister in Berlusconi's government, said he believed that Berlusconi had planted the device himself.
